content.text: Initial search terms will be `'intercept adjustment' 'in-sample error' evaluation`. This should yield relevant academic papers. The focus is on mean-residual adjustments and the evaluation of adjustments estimated from observed errors, especially the distinction between in-sample and out-of-sample error. The context also highlights the optimistic bias of in-sample error.

content.text: Considering classic literature on clinical prediction models and general regression, the focus is on identifying papers that discuss "in-sample" error versus generalization error, degrees of freedom, and methods for intercept adjustment. This includes papers that address mean residuals and optimistic bias within the context of model evaluation. Foundational works such as Steyerberg et al., Van Calster et al., Janssen et al., Harrell, and Copas are being examined.

Focus is now on specific papers: Efron (1986, 2004), Stone (1974), Copas (1983), Steyerberg et al. (2004, 2014) or Van Calster et al. (2016), Janssen et al. (2008), Harrell et al. (1996), Mallows (1973), Akaike (1974), Mosteller and Tukey (1977), Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman (2001/2009), Varma & Simon (2006), and Riley et al. (2019). The goal is to extract relevant concepts from these specific works.

content.text: Mean residual adjustments can improve model calibration, as evidenced by studies on updating clinical prediction models and defining calibration hierarchies. These adjustments, informed by empirical data, can enhance model performance in new patient populations.

Examining the provided citations, these studies address model validation, updating, and error estimation, which aligns with improving model calibration. The core themes involve sample size considerations for model validation, the impact of in-sample versus out-of-sample error, and techniques for mitigating bias in error estimation.

Mean-residual adjustments improve model calibration, evidenced by studies on updating clinical prediction models and calibration hierarchies, enhancing performance in new patient populations. These studies address model validation, updating, and error estimation, focusing on sample size for validation, in-sample versus out-of-sample error, and bias mitigation in error estimation.

Initial suspicion focused on fitted errors, specifically how observed mean residuals remove offsets on a fixed set of observations; this method doesn't generalize to new observations. The task aims to frame a finite instructional example, where a fixed predictor is offset from the target by a constant. Verification requires examining candidate papers for direct connections to intercept/mean-residual adjustments, in-sample error evaluation, degrees of freedom, and the distinction between fitted error and predictive evidence.

In-sample error rates are biased downward when evaluated on the training data, underestimating prediction error. Relevant citations connect in-sample fitting with degrees of freedom and penalties, showing fitting parameters creates optimism in-sample error fails to capture. Cross-validation formalizes a separation of model fitting and evaluation, avoiding the pitfalls of assessing a rule on the data used to construct it.

Mean calibration and intercept adjustments are formalized in the literature, with studies examining their impact on model performance and the distinction between in-sample fit and validation. Updating methods, including intercept adjustments, improve clinical prediction models in new patient populations by correcting mean offsets. The analysis of sample sizes shows adjustments on limited data lead to optimistic error estimates.

These citations directly address the core concerns. Harrell, Lee, and Mark (1996) expose the pitfalls of in-sample error. Mallows (1973) formalizes penalties for in-sample residual sum of squares, while Riley et al. (2021) examines out-of-sample validation and sample size. This literature provides a clear framework for understanding the limitations of in-sample error evaluation and the importance of cross-validation techniques.
